summary: This document updates RFC 5066. It tells the community that the EFM-CU-MIB module, used to manage Ethernet in the First Mile over copper, has moved from the concluded IETF working group to the IEEE 802.3 working group.

eli5.summary: A rulebook for a gadget changed owners. This note simply says who looks after the rulebook now.

questions: who maintains the ethernet in the first mile copper mib
who maintains the efm copper mib
subtitle: A short note saying that maintenance of the copper Ethernet management module moved from the IETF to the IEEE 802.3 working group.

tldr.problem: RFC 5066 defined a management module for copper Ethernet in the First Mile, but the IETF working group that owned it had concluded, so nobody there was left to maintain it.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC records that the EFM-CU-MIB module is frozen at its RFC 5066 form and that further work happens in the IEEE 802.3 working group as the IEEE8023-EFM-CU-MIB module. It also adds security considerations for the IF-CAP-STACK-MIB module, which stays with the IETF.
tldr.outcome: Operators can keep using EFM-CU-MIB, since both modules can coexist, but should expect new equipment to use the IEEE module.

today: RFC 7124 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5066, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. EFM-CU-MIB remains frozen at its RFC 5066 form, while IEEE8023-EFM-CU-MIB carries ongoing development.

sections.title: Why the Module Moved
sections.content:
RFC 5066 defines two MIB modules. EFM-CU-MIB has objects for managing 10PASS-TS and 2BASE-TL Ethernet in the First Mile Copper (EFMCu) interfaces. IF-CAP-STACK-MIB has objects describing the cross-connect capability of a managed device with multi-layer (stacked) interfaces.

When the IETF Ethernet Interfaces and Hub MIB working group (HUBMIB) concluded, responsibility for a MIB module for 2BASE-TL and 10PASS-TS interfaces went to the IEEE 802.3 working group. In 2011 the IEEE built the IEEE8023-EFM-CU-MIB module from the original EFM-CU-MIB. Its current revision is in IEEE Std 802.3.1-2013.
sections.eli5: The group that wrote the rulebook closed down, so a different group took over and wrote a new edition.

sections.title: The Management Framework
sections.content:
For an overview of the documents that make up the Internet-Standard Management Framework, the RFC points to section 7 of RFC 3410. It also states that the key words MUST, SHOULD and the like are to be read as described in RFC 2119.

The RFC itself defines no new MIB objects. It is an administrative update to RFC 5066.
sections.eli5: This part only tells you where the general rules for these gadgets are written down.

sections.title: Mapping Between the Two Modules
sections.content:
The IEEE module has the MODULE-IDENTITY ieee8023efmCuMIB, with an object identifier under the IEEE 802.3.1 MIBs sub-tree. The older module has the MODULE-IDENTITY efmCuMIB, with an object identifier under the mib-2 sub-tree.

The object names in the first version of IEEE8023-EFM-CU-MIB are identical to those in EFM-CU-MIB. Because the two modules have different OID values, they can coexist. A manager can control newer IEEE MIB-based devices alongside legacy IETF MIB-based devices.

Existing deployments of EFM-CU-MIB need not be upgraded, but operators should expect that new equipment will use the IEEE module.
sections.eli5: The two rulebooks use the same words but have different page numbers, so they never get mixed up and can sit on the same shelf.

sections.title: Who Maintains What
sections.content:
The EFM-CU-MIB defined in RFC 5066 becomes the last version of that module. All further development of the EFM Copper Interfaces MIB is done by the IEEE 802.3 working group in the IEEE8023-EFM-CU-MIB module. Requests and comments should go to the IEEE 802.3.1 task force, which is chartered with MIB development, through its mailing list.

IF-CAP-STACK-MIB was not transferred. It remains under IETF control and is maintained by the OPSAWG working group.
sections.eli5: Questions about the copper part now go to the new club. The part about stacked interfaces stays with the old one.

sections.title: Security of IF-CAP-STACK-MIB
sections.content:
The original RFC listed no security considerations for IF-CAP-STACK-MIB, so this one supplies them. The module has no objects with a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create, so correct implementations cannot be altered or have objects created through SNMP SET operations.

Some readable objects may still be sensitive. In particular, ifCapStackStatus and ifInvCapStackStatus can reveal the cross-connect capability of stacked interfaces, and so potentially the underlying hardware architecture. Access to them, even GET and NOTIFY, should be controlled, and values may even be encrypted in transit.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED. Implementations SHOULD provide the SNMPv3 security features, and those claiming SNMPv3 compliance MUST fully support authentication and privacy with the User-based Security Model and the AES cipher algorithm. They MAY also support the Transport Security Model with a secure transport such as SSH or TLS/DTLS.
sections.eli5: Even a read-only list can tell a snoop how your machine is built, so only trusted people should be allowed to look, and the messages should be locked.
